title: Elections Decided by a Glance
text:
In 2005 the Princeton psychologist Alexander Todorov and his students published a short paper with a startling claim. They took black and white head shots of the winners and runners-up in elections for the United States Senate and House of Representatives in 2000, 2002 and 2004. They showed the pairs of faces to students who did not recognize the candidates, and asked them a single question: which of the two looks more competent?

The quick judgments were remarkably predictive. The candidate rated as more competent had won about 70 percent of the Senate races and about two thirds of the House races. In one test the photos were shown for just one second, and the predictions were still accurate well above chance. For the 2004 elections, the ratings were collected before the votes were cast and still forecast most of the winners.

Other traits judged from faces, such as how trustworthy or likable a candidate seemed, predicted results much less well. The researchers concluded that voters' choices are shaped in part by fast, unreflective impressions of competence based on appearance alone.
lesson: We judge leaders by how competent they look long before we know what they can do. Slow down, and judge people you choose by their record.
people: Alexander Todorov, Anesu Mandisodza, Amir Goren, Crystal Hall
source: Todorov, A., Mandisodza, A. N., Goren, A., and Hall, C. C. (2005). Inferences of competence from faces predict election outcomes. Science, 308(5728), 1623-1626.
